prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how technological change, the task content of work and import competition reshape labour demand, the wage structure and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, as a single part. The exchange has changed how I would word the citation and how I would define the discovery, not the laureate set. The discovery is empirical. It shows that the demand for different kinds of labour moves with technology and trade in measurable ways, and that adjustment costs are persistent and concentrated in particular places. Katz's wage-structure and education-versus-technology work is the long-run benchmark. Autor's task-based evidence explains polarisation. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson import-competition design made local adjustment measurable. These are one question, studied with a shared standard of evidence. I now word the citation around what the evidence established and not around the whole task framework. That addresses the Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane attribution gap and leaves the magnitude of the China shock open. On maturity, the skill-premium and task work is about three decades old and the trade-shock evidence is over a decade old. All of it has been replicated and contested in the open, and the dispute over shift-share designs is part of how it was tested. On neighbouring prizes, I would count adjacency against a candidate only when the earlier citation covered the same discovery. Card 2021, Goldin 2023 and Acemoglu 2024 did not, on their written citations as I understand them. At most this is a modest timing consideration. I apply the same standard to B044, B037 and B017. The round-1 split is 5 for B044, 4 for B038 and 2 for B037. I treat that as information about which arguments have been examined, not as evidence of merit. B044 remains my first alternative and I would accept it if B038 cannot be defended on attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. A three-name cap cannot credit both Katz and Dorn alongside Autor and Hanson, and any choice excludes a real contributor. The task framework has contributors outside this ballot. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and shift-share identification, remain debated. The committee may reasonably see two discoveries, technology and trade, joined by Autor. If it does, a trade-shock award should credit Dorn, and a technology award would have a different laureate set. B044 has a more singular originating paper, and my preference for B038 rests on a judgement that its broader evidence and policy relevance outweigh that advantage. I could be wrong about this. My field is close to B038, and I may be over-weighting familiarity with the evidence standard.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first. She gives B038 less weight on maturity than B044 because shift-share identification and the persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. She says she would support B038 if the committee found a convincing way to credit Dorn.
responses.response: I take the Dorn point seriously and cannot resolve it within the cap. Autor, Hanson, Katz and Dorn is four names, and the choice between Katz and Dorn depends on whether the award is defined as labour demand broadly or as the trade shock narrowly. On maturity I distinguish between what is established and what is still debated. The existence of persistent, geographically concentrated adjustment costs has held up across settings and specifications. The size of the effects and the best identification strategy are still contested. The shift-share econometrics has itself been developed over the past decade, which I read as a sign the evidence has been tested, not as immaturity. I have not independently re-verified that literature. If the committee narrows the award to the trade shock, I would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson over Autor and Hanson, because the cap allows Dorn and a trade-shock citation should not omit him. I still prefer the broader award, because the narrower one drops the wage-structure evidence that gives the shock its interpretation.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B044 first. She says B038's credit boundary is blurred by neighbouring prizes and by two distinct strands, and she wants the argument made on which strand carries the discovery, not on combining them.
responses.response: My answer is that the discovery is the demand for labour and who bears the adjustment, and the two strands are two ways of identifying shifts in it. Technological change and import exposure are both measured at the level of tasks, industries and places, and Katz's wage-structure work is the benchmark against which both are read. I would not claim the whole task framework, which is why the citation now names the empirical evidence. On neighbouring prizes I read the 2021, 2023 and 2024 citations as adjacent and not duplicative, as I argued in round 1. I agree that B044 has the more singular originating paper. But it also leaves out Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, so neither candidate has a boundary free of dispute. Where we differ is in weighing a cleaner core against a broader body of tested evidence. I regard that as a difference of weighting, not of facts.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B037 first. He notes that Katz also appears on B045 and that any B038 award should state which of his contributions it recognises. He also says that more weight on direct empirical confirmation would favour B038 over B037.
responses.response: I accept both points. The Katz contribution I credit is the work on wage structure and the race between education and technology. His work on intergenerational mobility under B045 is a separate body of research and not part of my citation, which refers only to the wage structure and labour demand. I rank B045 fifth in my opening, but I do not propose it here and would not want the B038 citation to be read as covering it. On empirical confirmation, I weigh it heavily because of my own field. I find the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution clean and the mechanism foundational. Because much of its support is indirect and model-based, I would rank it below a body of work that has been tested in transparent designs. I could not judge the Kiyotaki-Moore evidence against the 2022 background from what I have in front of me, so I hold this view with uncertainty.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) ranks B037 first. His round-1 B038 trio was Autor and Hanson only, because Katz's skill-biased-change work overlaps with the 2023 prize and the task framework builds on Acemoglu and Levy-Murnane. He kept B038 out of his preferred configuration until a principled boundary was agreed.
responses.response: Autor and Hanson is a defensible, cleaner version, and I said in round 1 that I could weigh it. I prefer Katz for two reasons. He anchors the long-run skill-premium benchmark, and without him the citation becomes mainly a trade-shock award. On the 2023 overlap, I read Goldin's prize as being for women's labour-market outcomes over the long run. The Katz-Goldin work on education and technology is adjacent to it, and the wage-structure evidence was not the object recognised. I would count that as a modest timing consideration and not as a scientific objection. As a principled boundary I propose this. The award is for the empirical evidence on how technology and trade shift labour demand and local adjustment. It does not claim the theoretical task framework. It credits the three authors who carry the wage-structure, task-evidence and local-adjustment strands. If the committee will not accept that boundary, I would move to the narrower trade-shock version, not to Autor and Hanson with an unclear scope.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees B038 as one achievement on labour demand or as two strands that should be recognised separately, which determines whether Katz or Dorn belongs in the third slot.
How large and persistent the China-shock effects are, and whether shift-share identification is a maturity concern or only a matter of citation wording.
How far the neighbouring 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes should lower the marginal case. I read them as adjacency, but members who weigh them more heavily may be right.
Whether the B044 boundary (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum) is more or less defensible than the B038 boundary. I weigh breadth of tested evidence against a cleaner core and could be wrong.

B017 is a weaker second alternative than it was at my opening, because Krusell, Enflo and Teorell raised identification and 2024-overlap concerns that I find fair. I have not independently verified any citation, impact or priority claims, and my assessment rests on the supplied files and my own general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is documented in my supplied profile, nor to the named alternatives on B044 or B017. I work in empirical labour economics, so B038 is close to my field. I treat that proximity as a reason for caution and not as evidence of merit. As chair I delivered the 2021 presentation speech on Card, Angrist and Imbens, and a 2013 paper of mine on class size is cited in that scientific background. That is a connection to a neighbouring prize and not to any credited name here. My Stockholm overlap with the IIES macro group was institutional only. Katz also appears on B045, which is not part of my configuration. I see no need for recusal on any ballot and do not adjudicate others' disclosures.
